title: Democratizing Foundations of Problem-Solving with AI: A Breadth-First Search Curriculum for Middle School Students
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how to broaden access to AI education by embedding foundational AI problem-solving ideas into regular K–12 subject instruction rather than offering stand-alone AI activities. Specifically, it asks whether middle school students can learn Breadth-First Search (BFS) as a concrete example of AI reasoning when the content is integrated into a science unit on virus transmission and contact tracing.

The intervention was a seven-day, co-designed curriculum delivered in a rural public middle school health science course in the United States. The curriculum combined an interactive Snap!-based environment (I-SAIL) with unplugged tracing tasks, map-based pathfinding, and science applications involving disease spread and contact networks. Students practiced BFS through scaffolded simulation activities, then applied the idea in paper-based and hands-on science contexts. The study collected pre/post assessments, student work artifacts, and a teacher interview.

Results showed significant gains in students’ BFS understanding from pre- to post-assessment, and most students could correctly identify a shortest path on the unplugged worksheet, though many had difficulty documenting every procedural step. The teacher reported that the module fit well within the existing science curriculum and helped students connect AI reasoning to science concepts. The paper concludes that AI problem-solving can be productively taught in ordinary subject classrooms when curricula are carefully designed, scaffolded, and co-developed with teachers.

identified_tools.name: CAI (General)
identified_tools.description: Computer-assisted instruction or AI-supported instructional system used in K–12 learning contexts.
identified_tools.use_case: The paper describes a classroom curriculum and interactive learning environment for teaching Breadth-First Search (BFS) as an AI problem-solving procedure within middle school science instruction. The system is i-SAIL, a Snap!-based environment, but the paper does not study a named commercial AI product or an LLM chatbot.

findings.finding_summary: Students showed improved performance on a matched five-item BFS knowledge assessment after the four core I-SAIL activities. Mean score increased from 0.683 (SD=0.219) pre-test to 0.790 (SD=0.232) post-test, with the improvement statistically significant in a paired t-test and Wilcoxon signed-rank test. The within-subject effect was moderate (Cohen’s dz=0.453).
findings.measure: Matched pre/post BFS knowledge assessment (5 multiple-choice items)

findings.finding_summary: On a paper-based BFS tracing worksheet completed after the I-SAIL activities, 64.5% of students accurately identified the shortest path to the goal state. However, many students omitted intermediate steps and had incomplete exploration-order records, indicating partial procedural understanding.
findings.measure: Paper-based BFS tracing worksheet accuracy and step-by-step procedural completeness

quality_tier_rationale: This is a classroom implementation study with pre/post assessment and interview data, but it is not an experimental evaluation of a named AI product. The evidence is mixed-methods and observational, so it fits a lower-than-experimental tier.
impact_tier_rationale: The reported learning gain on the BFS assessment is moderate (dz=0.453), which meets the threshold for medium impact. The worksheet results suggest useful but incomplete procedural learning, so overall impact is positive but bounded.
